Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. New York Democratic Governor Kathy
Hochul appointed State Attorney General Letitia James to be a special prosecutor to investigate
gang rape allegations at Cornell University. Aurora Berry from member station WSKG reports
the governor says she made the decision after learning troubling details about how authorities
handled the case.
It came out this week and NPR confirmed that the woman told university police back in 2024
she was raped by a group of fraternity members. The governor pointed to that revelation and
to a statement by Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten that he never
saw a transcript of her 2024 interview with police. Instead, he relied on a six-page report
from campus police and did not charge anyone with a crime. At the press conference, Hochul
said that the woman was failed by institutions that were supposed to protect her.
Aurora Berry from WSKG reporting, a former Miami congressman has been sentenced to ten
years in prison for a secret $50 million lobbying campaign for Venezuela during President Trump's
first term. Republican David Rivera is a longtime friend of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
He was found guilty in May of failing to register as a foreign agent and conspiracy to commit
money laundering. Rubio testified he had no idea it was going on and that he felt betrayed.
An energy department employee accused of providing support to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels made
his first court appearance today. Northwest Public Broadcasting's Eric Bengal reports.
An FBI investigation into Ashton Hamid Elabudi began when he allegedly bought chemicals and
materials often used to make homemade explosives. The 51-year-old Richland, Washington resident
allegedly sought to help the Houthis, the Iran-backed paramilitary group that has taken
control of much of Yemen. The U.S. has designated the Houthis a foreign terrorist organization.
Elabudi, who worked for the U.S. Department of Energy as an electrical engineer, allegedly
traveled to Yemen without authorization. The FBI says Elabudi wanted to help the Houthis
improve their communications capabilities. A detention hearing is scheduled for next
week. For NPR News, I'm Eric Bengal in Walla Walla, Washington.
For nearly half a century, the federal government has said segregating people with disabilities
and institutions is in most cases an act of discrimination, but the Trump administration
disagrees, NPR's Janaki Mehta reports. The Justice Department began shifting its
position back in June, saying states didn't have to integrate people with disabilities
into their communities to follow the law. It all culminated in a court case last week
when a federal judge agreed to strip the concept — even the word "integration" — out
of federal rules. That doesn't change laws that protect integration, but experts like
Jennifer Mathis, a disability rights lawyer, say it sends a clear message.
It is a signal to states. The federal government thinks they have permission to go institutionalize
people. Although the law hasn't changed, federal enforcement
already has. This is NPR News.
A Venezuelan delivery driver, who was shot by a federal immigration agent in Texas, has
had surgery to remove the bullet lodged in his back. Authorities say that nearly two
weeks ago, the agent shot 28-year-old Wilbur Rafael Garces Perez after he struck an agent
with the side mirror of a vehicle while trying to evade arrest.
Maryland is now the first state in the nation to pass a law restricting the use of consumers'
personal data to charge them more for groceries. NPR's Windsor Johnston has more on what the
law bans and what it still allows. The restrictions cover larger grocery stores
and third-party delivery services. They target personalized markups based on information
about the customer. But there's an exception for voluntary loyalty programs, which have
given shoppers discounts for decades. University of Chicago marketing professor Jean-Pierre
Dubay says that history helps sellers gauge what people are willing to spend.
"It's not a pricing discussion, it's a privacy discussion. People are worried that things
they thought were private information about themselves might now be not just affecting
what they're charged, but just marketing in general."
Other states, including New York and New Jersey, are considering similar laws. In Maryland,
businesses get 45 days after a violation notice to fix the problem.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
Major League Baseball introduced robot umpires this year, allowing hitters, catchers and
pitchers to have a computer automatically review balls and strikes. Now that the regular
season is over, robot umpires overturned 54 percent of challenged calls. The Cincinnati
Reds benefited the most from overturns, and catchers were more successful than batters
and pitchers. This is NPR News.
